title: India Bets on a 'Digital Tourism Stack' to Unify Its Fragmented Travel Market
excerpt: The Ministry of Tourism and ONDC have launched the National Digital Tourism Stack, an open, AI-first infrastructure meant to make 23,000 homestays and experiences discoverable and bookable across platforms by 2028.
body:
• The Ministry of Tourism and ONDC have launched the National Digital Tourism Stack, an open digital infrastructure meant to make India's homestays, guides, experiences, and transport services discoverable, trustworthy, and bookable through multiple platforms.
  • For your next India trip: flights, hotels, cabs, boat rides, and even a temple 'aarti' could be booked and paid for through one interface in your preferred language — a pilot runs January–June 2027, with a nationwide rollout beginning July 2027 and 23,000 experiences and homestays targeted by the end of 2028.
  • The design is AI-first: Tourism Secretary Bhuvnesh Kumar says AI will be the front end, supporting AI-led interfaces and personal digital agents as travel discovery models shift.
  • More than 1,000 tourism experiences — including 170 ASI monuments and 29 museums — are already transacting on the ONDC network.

India launches its tourism 'stack'

India now has an official blueprint for digitizing the long tail of its tourism industry. The Ministry of Tourism, together with the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), launched the National Digital Tourism Stack (NDTS) on World Tourism Day — September 27, 2026 — at a function at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, presided over by Union Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat. It was built with the International Centre for DPI Innovation and Advancement.

The stack is not another travel-booking website. It is shared digital public infrastructure — an open layer that connects destinations, tourism businesses, and travelers across participating digital platforms. The model is "list once, reach multiple platforms": a homestay owner in Ladakh, a guide in Hampi, or a boat operator in Varanasi publishes an offering once and becomes visible and bookable across every participating app, without building a separate integration for each one.

"Currently, flights, hotels, cabs, boat rides, or even an 'aarti' at a temple, et cetera, need to be booked through different websites. This fragmentation makes the process a digitally painful experience for a tourist planning to visit places."

— Bhuvnesh Kumar, Union Tourism Secretary

A fragmented market gets a unifying layer

The problem the stack targets is one every India traveler recognizes. While big hotels, airlines, and marquee attractions run sophisticated online distribution, thousands of smaller businesses and locally run experiences still trade through a patchwork of websites, social media, offline bookings, and intermediaries. Skift notes this fragmentation is precisely why the concept could matter most in India: the country's tourism supply is overwhelmingly made up of small providers that the current system underserves.

According to the Entrepreneur India report on the launch, tourism contributed 5.22% of India's GDP and supported 8.46 crore jobs in 2023–24 — yet much of that supply remains fragmented across offline and digital channels. The NDTS is meant to fix that with shared rails for verified identities and supplier credentials, search and discovery, payments, ratings, and grievance redressal.

The vision, in Kumar's words, is "One ticket, One pass" — to "bring all of India together in a single journey." The ministry says it will act as catalyst and lead, working with states and Union Territories to curate and validate experiences, and will set up a steering committee inviting the tourism industry to partner in the initiative.

What changes for travelers, platforms, and small operators

For travelers, the infrastructure is intended to bring stays, experiences, destinations, routes, and last-mile mobility closer together through shared digital rails, reducing friction across discovery, payments, and the rest of the journey. The ministry's stated aim is that a tourist visiting a big city or a small town can plan and travel "easy, safe, and in one's preferred language" — discovering more of India, traveling with confidence, booking and paying easily, and reducing paperwork.

For platforms, the stack removes the need for one-to-one integrations: build once against the open network and gain access to the country's tourism inventory. For small operators, it is market access — a homestay or experience that today lives only on a Facebook page or a word-of-mouth network becomes discoverable to domestic and international demand through multiple apps. The target: 23,000 tourism experiences and homestays (14,000 experiences plus 9,000 homestays) onboarded, discoverable, and bookable by the end of 2028.

There is an early proof point: more than 1,000 tourism experiences, including 170 Archaeological Survey of India monuments and 29 museums, are already transacting on the ONDC network, according to the Ministry and ONDC.

What it means for diaspora travelers

NRIs planning India trips face this fragmentation more acutely than most. A typical visit mixes big-city logistics with home-region experiences — the family homestay in Kerala, a local guide in Rajasthan, a dawn aarti in Varanasi, a boat ride in Kashmir — and booking those pieces today means juggling WhatsApp threads, agency intermediaries, and sites that vary by state and operator. A single unified stack with verified credentials, ratings, grievance redressal, and payment rails designed for one language-agnostic interface would collapse that work into one planning session.

Second- and third-generation visitors, who often lack the family networks that route around the fragmentation, stand to gain the most: discoverability of lesser-known destinations and vetted small operators is exactly the gap the ministry is targeting. The rollout timeline gives overseas travelers something concrete to plan around — the pilot runs January through June 2027, with nationwide supply onboarding from July 2027, so a winter-2027 or 2028 trip could be the first to ride the full stack.

What's next

The roadmap is phased: preparation and development runs October through December 2026, the pilot January to June 2027, and scale-out from July 2027 to December 2028 with a nationwide supply onboarding drive, per Kumar. Execution is the risk — open digital infrastructure only works if enough platforms and providers join, and if state-level curation keeps quality high.

Watch the pilot's scope and the steering committee's industry participation. On the same World Tourism Day occasion, the ministry also launched the "Mission for Redistribution of Tourism Demand Promotion of Lesser-known Destinations" and Dekho Apna Desh 2.0 — bookable itineraries covering accommodation, transport, meals, and local experiences that route demand toward lesser-known places, with opportunities for artisans, self-help groups, and local guides. Together they signal a government intent to shift India's tourism economy from a handful of overloaded circuits to the full breadth of the country — with the digital stack as the rails.

nri_angle: NRIs booking home-region homestays, guides, and experiences face India's booking fragmentation most acutely; a single verified stack with unified payments in their preferred language would collapse that planning work — and second-generation visitors without family networks gain the most.
author: Diaspora Desk
